item.title: Using the Raspberry Pi Sense HAT with Pi4J Drivers
item.description:
Using the Raspberry Pi Sense HAT with Pi4J Drivers

20260701 - Video by Igor De Souza

The Sense HAT packs an 8×8 RGB LED matrix, environmental sensors (temperature, humidity, and pressure), motion sensors (accelerometer, gyroscope, and magnetometer), and a small joystick onto a single Raspberry Pi expansion board. In this video, Igor De Souza shows how Java developers can talk to all of that hardware through Pi4J Drivers, the companion library to Pi4J.

item.title: From Breadboard Chaos to a Real PCB: Designing the Pi4J Smoke Test Board
item.description:
From breadboard chaos to a real PCB: designing the Pi4J smoke test board

20260625 - Video with Frank Delporte

Testing a Java I/O library properly means testing it on real hardware. For Pi4J that means running the smoke test: a setup with two BMP/BME280 sensors and a tangle of GPIO-to-GPIO jumper wires that has to be rebuilt by hand every session. This video tells the story of board number 0001: turning that breadboard setup into a proper PCB.

item.title: Validating Pi4J V4 on Real Hardware with the Ikalogic Logic Analyser
item.description:
Validating Pi4J V4 on real hardware, catching bugs, and exploring the Ikalogic logic analyser

20260330 - Video with Tom Aarts

Pi4J contributor Tom Aarts joins Frank Delporte for a hands-on session focused on hardware testing in Pi4J V4. Tom has been a long-time contributor to the Pi4J ecosystem. He added example devices, improved core code by finding gaps through real-world usage, and most recently designed the Pi4J Smoke Test hardware setup that makes integration testing on real Raspberry Pi hardware practical and repeatable.

item.title: Let's Smoke Some Food with Pi4J, Vaadin, and Quarkus
item.description:
Let’s smoke some food with Pi4J, Vaadin, and Quarkus

20260319 - Live Stream

Live stream with Matti Tahvonen and Frank Delporte with the smell of smoked food and fresh Java code! Matti from the Vaadin team shows a project that started as a Raspberry Pi side project and turned into a full-blown IoT application. He has built a smoker controller — yes, an actual BBQ smoker — with Pi4J V4, Vaadin for the UI, and Quarkus on the backend. So we can now officially say that Pi4J V4 has been smoke-tested in production…

item.title: Controlling Electronics with Java 25 and the FFM API using Pi4J V4
item.description:
Controlling Electronics with Java 25 and the FFM API using Pi4J V4

20260306 - Live Stream

Live stream with Nick Gritsenko and Frank Delporte about the Foreign Function and Memory (FFM) API that got introduced in Java 22, and how it was used to create a new plugin for the Pi4J library. This will help to bring electronics programming with Java to many more boards and help to simplify the Pi4J project.

item.title: Foreign Function & Memory API Brings Modern Java to the Raspberry Pi
item.description:
The Wait is Over: Foreign Function & Memory FFM API brings modern Java to the Raspberry Pi

20251009 - Recording of the talk at Devoxx Belgium by Frank Delporte

All the links of the presentation are available on this blog post.

Since 2012, Pi4J has enabled Java to control electronic components connected to the Raspberry Pi’s GPIO pins. However, both Java and the Raspberry Pi have evolved significantly since then. Supporting new hardware has been a challenge, requiring multiple implementations in the Pi4J library with complex code based on the Java Native Interface (JNI) and Java Native Access (JNA).

item.title: Improving the Vaadin+Spring+Pi4J Demo Application with Matti Tahvonen
item.description:
Live Stream Coding

Improving the Vaadin+Spring+Pi4J demo application with Matti Tahvonen

2025-09-24, by Frank Delporte

During a live stream coding session, Matti Tahvonen and Frank Delporte updated an existing Vaadin+Spring+Pi4J demo application to use the latest version of the libraries and Java 25. It’s a demo application created a few years ago to be used during presentations at conferences. Of course, everything evolves, so a big update and refactoring was needed.

(Sorry for the hiccups in the first minutes, the network connection dropped a few times…)

item.title: Having Fun with LED Strips with Java on the Raspberry Pi
item.description:
Having fun with LED strips with Java on the Raspberry Pi

20231012 - Live Stream

Frank Delporte and Robert von Burg (aka Eitch) take a look at examples using JBang and Pixelblaze, which are described on the Pi4J website at https://www.pi4j.com/examples/jbang/pixelblaze_output_expander/.

This was our first live stream using restream.io to see if we could create tutorials like this. This went smoothly for the first 44 minutes, and then I lost connection with Robert. But luckily, at that time, we had already explained almost everything we wanted to tell ;-)

item.title: Controlling Electronics with Java and Pi4J through a Web Interface
item.description:
Controlling Electronics with Java and Pi4J through a web interface

20230822 - J-Spring, The Netherlands

Java is not only the server language running on heavy machines! You can do amazing stuff with it on a small single-board computer and gain new knowledge simultaneously, like controlling electronic components and different communication protocols.

item.title: Building Smart Devices using Java on the Raspberry Pi
item.description:
Building Smart Devices using Java on the Raspberry Pi

An intro to Pi4J by Frank Delporte

20121014 - Devoxx Belgium

A Raspberry Pi is a full Linux PC with a small form factor and a low price of between 6 and 95€. And of course, you can run Java on it. The same kind of JVM applications you know, love, and use on heavy machines can also be used on the Raspberry Pi. “Write once, run everywhere”? Ah yes, that’s the promise of Java! But this small board has some additional possibilities you will not find on that fancy server you are running somewhere in the cloud.

item.title: Java, JavaFX, and Electronics Programming on the Raspberry Pi
item.description:
Java, JavaFX, and electronics programming on the Raspberry Pi

20210211 - PL JUGs United, Online

Java, JavaFX and a Raspberry Pi are an ideal combination for any project where you want to connect software and hardware (LEDs, buttons, sensors…) with a beautiful, easy-to-use user interface. In this talk, we will go through the process of building some example Java applications which use electronic components connected to a Raspberry Pi.

item.title: The Future of Java on Raspberry Pi
item.description:
The Future of Java on Raspberry Pi

Java, JavaFX, Raspberry Pi and Electronics

20210207 - Fosdem “Friends of OpenJDK devroom”, Online

Java on the Raspberry Pi is still a controversial topic, but recent evolutions of both the JDK and OpenJFX have proven they are a perfect match! In this talk we will look into some examples and discuss what could be the next steps.
